subject: Science
central_question: How are electric current, potential difference and resistance related, and how do resistor combinations determine heating, power and electrical energy use in circuits?
in_scope_units: Electric current, charge flow, electric circuit, conventional current and measurement by an ammeter.
Electric potential difference, work per unit charge and measurement by a voltmeter.
Conventional symbols used in circuit diagrams.
Ohm's law and the relationship among potential difference, current and resistance.
Factors affecting resistance and the concept of electrical resistivity.
Equivalent resistance of resistors connected in series.
Equivalent resistance of resistors connected in parallel and advantages of parallel circuits.
Heating effect of electric current, Joule's law and practical applications including heating devices, bulbs and fuses.
Electric power, electrical energy, watt, kilowatt-hour and cost of energy consumption.
banned_topics: Magnetic field produced by current, motors, generators and electromagnetic induction, which belong to the next chapter.
Detailed semiconductor electronics and alternating-current circuit analysis.
Detailed domestic wiring beyond the fuse application stated in this chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: Conventional current flows in the same direction as electrons in a metal wire.
known_pitfalls.correction: Conventional current is taken opposite to the direction of electron flow.

known_pitfalls.claim: An ammeter is connected in parallel and a voltmeter in series.
known_pitfalls.correction: An ammeter is connected in series with the circuit, while a voltmeter is connected in parallel across the points being measured.

known_pitfalls.claim: Ohm's law is valid under all conditions.
known_pitfalls.correction: For a given metallic conductor, potential difference is proportional to current only when temperature remains the same.

known_pitfalls.claim: A thicker wire has greater resistance than a thinner wire of the same material and length.
known_pitfalls.correction: Resistance is inversely proportional to area of cross-section, so a thicker wire has lower resistance.

known_pitfalls.claim: The equivalent resistance of parallel resistors is larger than every branch resistance.
known_pitfalls.correction: The equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is smaller than the smallest individual resistance.

known_pitfalls.claim: Electricity bills charge for electrons consumed.
known_pitfalls.correction: Electrons are not consumed; the bill is for electrical energy supplied to move charges through appliances.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Examples 11.1 and 11.2 for current as charge per time and potential difference as work per charge.
Use NCERT Activity 11.1 and Examples 11.3-11.6 for Ohm's law, resistance and resistivity.
Use NCERT Activities 11.4-11.6 and Examples 11.7-11.9 for series, parallel and mixed resistor combinations.
Use NCERT Examples 11.10-11.11 and the in-text heating questions for Joule's law and practical heating applications.
Use NCERT Examples 11.12-11.13 and Exercises Q15-Q17 for electric power and commercial energy use.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES contain Questions 1-18, covering resistance, resistor combinations, heating, power, energy and practical material choices.
